classification.difficultyReason: Routine differentiate, factorise and solve. The twist is that $y'=3(x-2)^2$ gives a single stationary point where $f''=0$, so the student must use a sign test to see it is a horizontal inflection and not an extremum. It is a little harder than a standard classification and has no endpoint comparison.

content.prompt: Find the stationary points of $y=x^3-6x^2+12x-5$ and determine their nature.

answer.short: One stationary point, $(2,3)$, which is a horizontal point of inflection.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y'&=3x^2-12x+12\\y'&=3(x-2)^2\\3(x-2)^2&=0\\x&=2\\y(2)&=8-24+24-5\\y(2)&=3\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}y''&=6x-12\\y''(2)&=0\end{align*}$$
The second derivative test is inconclusive, so check the sign of $y'$ either side of $x=2$:
$$\begin{align*}y'(1)&=3>0\\y'(3)&=3>0\end{align*}$$
The gradient does not change sign, so $(2,3)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
